# 2.6 – Equivalent Expressions {.unnumbered}

When you visit another country, you might hear the same word said in different ways. *Hello*, *hola*, *bonjour* — all mean the same thing, but they look and sound different.

Math is like that too. An idea can be written many different ways. $2(x+3)$ and $2x+6$ look different, but they both “say” the same thing. We call such pairs **equivalent expressions**. 

In this lesson, you’ll learn how to recognize when expressions are equivalent by simplifying, using substitution, and thinking logically. This idea is a big deal in Algebra — especially when we start solving equations in Unit 3.

---

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I can say what it means for two expressions to be equivalent.
- [ ] I can prove equivalence by rewriting one expression to match the other.
- [ ] I can tell the difference between testing and proving equivalence.
:::

### 2.6.1 – What Does “Equivalent” Mean?

Two expressions are **equivalent** if they have the **same value for every input** (for all allowed values of the variable).

They do **not** have to look the same. What matters is the value you get when you plug in the **same** input.

---

**Example 1 — Two forms, same value**

Compare

$$
A(x)=3(x+4)\quad\text{and}\quad B(x)=3x+12.
$$

Try two easy inputs (we’ll use $x=0$ and $x=5$):

| $x$ |       $A(x)=3(x+4)$ |    $B(x)=3x+12$ |
| --: | ------------------: | --------------: |
|   0 | $3(0+4)=3\cdot4=12$ | $3\cdot0+12=12$ |
|   5 | $3(5+4)=3\cdot9=27$ | $3\cdot5+12=27$ |

The outputs match both times. This is **evidence** that the expressions mean the same thing.

---

**Example 2 — A pair that is *not* equivalent**

Compare

$$
C(x)=4x+1 \quad\text{and}\quad D(x)=4(x+1).
$$

Try $x=2$:

$$
C(2)=4(\textcolor{red}{2})+1=8+1=9
\qquad
D(2)=4(\textcolor{red}{2}+1)=4\cdot3=12.
$$

Different outputs → these two are **not** equivalent.

---

**Example 3 — Matching once doesn’t settle it**

Sometimes two expressions match at some inputs but not at others.

$$
P(x)=x \quad\text{and}\quad Q(x)=x^2.
$$

* $x=0:\; P(0)=0,\; Q(0)=0$ (match)
* $x=1:\; P(1)=1,\; Q(1)=1$ (match)
* $x=2:\; P(2)=2,\; Q(2)=4$ (no match)

So matching at one or two inputs is **only evidence**, not a guarantee.

---

:::{.you-try title="Check two inputs and say what you found"}
Pick **two** easy inputs (0, 1, 2, or $-1$) for each pair. Compute both outputs each time. Decide whether you have **evidence of equivalence** or a **counterexample**.

1. $x+x+x$ and $3x$
2. $5(x-2)$ and $5x-10$
3. $2x+3$ and $2(x+3)$
:::

:::{.remember}
**Sentence frame (to explain your result):**
“At $x=\_\_$, the first expression equals \_\_\_ and the second equals \_\_\_. So I have evidence they **are / are not** equivalent.”
:::

---

:::{.think title="Why “for every input” matters"}

* One mismatch is enough to show two expressions are **not** equivalent.
* Many matches give **evidence**, but not a proof.

In the next sections, you’ll use algebra you already know (combining like terms, distributing, factoring) to **show** that two expressions are the same for **every** input.
:::
